title: Thomas More and His Daughter Margaret
text:
Thomas More, lawyer, author of Utopia and later Lord Chancellor of England, ran a household school at his home for his children. In an age when few women learned more than to read, he insisted his daughters be educated as thoroughly as his son: Latin, Greek, logic, philosophy, astronomy. His eldest daughter, Margaret, became one of the most learned women in England. Erasmus admired her, and she translated one of his works from Latin into English.

More wrote her affectionate letters praising her writing. She married William Roper, who later wrote More's biography.

When More refused to swear the oath recognizing Henry VIII's new marriage and break with Rome, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London in 1534. Margaret was allowed to visit him and tried, with all her learning, to persuade him to take the oath and save his life. He would not, but their letters from this time are full of tenderness.

According to William Roper's account, after More was condemned in July 1535, Margaret forced her way through the guards on the Tower wharf to embrace and kiss her father in front of everyone. On the eve of his execution, More wrote her a final letter with a piece of coal. He was beheaded on 6 July 1535. Tradition says Margaret recovered his head from London Bridge and kept it until her own death.
lesson: Educating daughters as fully as sons is a gift that can outlast a parent's life. Loving someone does not mean agreeing with every choice they make.
people: Thomas More, Margaret Roper, William Roper, Erasmus
location: Chelsea and the Tower of London, England (UK)
source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c. 1556); The Correspondence of Sir Thomas More
caveat: The story of the head comes from later tradition.
